rows.change: explanation: 62% -> 52% at 20°C (textbook error; the cards already say 52%)

before.explanation: A worked example shows air holding a fixed amount of water vapour cooling from 100% relative humidity at 10°C to 62% at 20°C and just 28% at 30°C. The absolute moisture content never changes in that example - only the temperature does - which is exactly why relative humidity falls as temperature rises: warmer air can hold more moisture, so the same vapour represents a shrinking fraction of what the air could now hold.

rows.change: explanation: 62% -> 52% at 20°C (textbook error; the cards already say 52%)

before.explanation: A parcel of air holding a constant amount of water vapour has its relative humidity fall from 100% at 10°C to 62% at 20°C and 28% at 30°C - purely because warming raises the air's capacity to hold moisture without adding any more of it. Relative humidity is the ratio of actual to maximum possible moisture at that temperature, so raising the temperature alone, with nothing else changing, must push that ratio down.

after.explanation: A parcel of air holding a constant amount of water vapour has its relative humidity fall from 100% at 10°C to 52% at 20°C and 28% at 30°C - purely because warming raises the air's capacity to hold moisture without adding any more of it.
